bioprojects.title: Isolation and in vitro culture of Lacazia loboi: morphology, physiology and complete genome sequencing

description.comment: Lobomycosis is a dermal mycosis, presenting nodular, keloid-like, single or multiple, cutaneous diffuse lesions on the skin of affected patients. Since the report of the first case, in 1931, described by Dr. Jorge Lobo in an Amazonian rubber tapper, this disease was thought to be restricted to humans living at the Amazon Region. However, in 1971, the first case in an Atlantic bottle-nosed dolphin was described, and in 2008 the first two autochthonous African cases were described. During the last decade, it became clear that lobomycosis is an emerging human and dolphin disease, not restricted to the Amazon Region, and possibly related to environmental stressors, which could lead to the death of some dolphins. The inability to cultivate the causative agent of lobomycosis impaired research on the biology of the fungus, creating different nomenclatures over the years, varying from Glenosporella loboi, through Paracoccidioides loboi (Fonseca Filho & Area Leao, 1940), and more recently Lacazia loboi; on the classification of the disease, leading to terms as lobomycosis like-disease (LLD); and on the development of new drugs, resulting in the absence of a drug-of-choice for the treatment of lobomycosis. We cultivated this fungus in vitro, and based on its in vitro and in vivo behavior, on cellular biology data and on the complete genome sequence assembly of one of our strains it is possible to conclude that Lacazia loboi is related in fact to the another already know genera Candida under the phylum Ascomycota, and therefore, based on our complete genome data, the new nomenclature Candida loboi is proposed.

assembly_info.comments:
Background:
The Crithidia fasciculata (strain/isolate Cf-C1) was obtained from Dr. Larry Simpson, University of California, Los Angeles. Genomic DNA was prepared by CsCl/Ethidium bromide density gradient centrifugation to minimize the amount of kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA, and was provided by Drs. Natalia Akopyants, Lon-Fye Lye and Stephen Beverley, Washington University School of Medicine. The Crithidia fasciculata 14.0 assembly was assembled with Celera (v8.0) using 30X of PacBio long reads derived from an initial 130X coverage of PacBio reads, which were corrected by ECtools (v1.0) using the 13.3.5 reference assembly. The Celera assembly was further corrected using Quiver, and then ordered and oriented into pseudochromosomes by alignment to Leishmania major friedlin at the Myler lab. Finally, the assembly was gap-filled with PBJelly (v14.9.9), and error-corrected with icorn2. The final 14.0 assembly is made up of a total of 31 pseudochromosomes with an N50 pseudochromosome length of 1.3Mb and an N50 contig length of over 920Kb. The 427 unplaced contigs comprise nearly 8.7Mb of sequence. The assembled genome spans over 40Mb.
This work was supported by NIH grant AI29646 to SMB and by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW, Director of The Genome Institute at Washington University.
For questions regarding this Crithidia fasciculata 14.0 assembly please contact Dr. Wesley Warren, Washington University School of Medicine (wwarren@genome.wustl.edu). Downloads of the sequence data are available via the TriTrypDB genome browser server. Funding for the sequence characterization of the Crithidia fasciculata genome was provided by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Source DNA can be obtained by mailing: Stephen M. Beverley, Ph.D. Marvin A. Brennecke Professor and Head of Molecular Microbiology Department of Molecular Microbiology Campus Box 8230 Washington University School of Medicine 660 S. Euclid Ave. St. Louis, MO 63110 USA

bioprojects.title: Endotrypanum monterogeii strain:LV88 Genome sequencing and assembly
Pathogenomics of Trypanosomatid Parasites
NHGRI Large Scale Sequencing Program for Organismal Sequencing

assembly_info.comments:
Background:
The Endotrypanum monterogeii LV88 strain was provided by Dr. Michael Chance, Liverpool, as described (A. H. Lopes, D.M. Iovannisci, M. Petrillo-Peixoto, D. McMahon-Pratt, & S.M. Beverley (1990), Molec. Biochem. Parasitol. 40: 151-162). It was isolated from a Choloepus hoffmani sloth in Costa Rica.
Genomic DNA was prepared by CsCl/Ethidium bromide density gradient centrifugation to minimize the amount of kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA, and was provided by Drs. Natalia Akopyants and Stephen Beverley, Washington University School of Medicine.
Total sequence coverage of 454 instrument reads was 50X (Fragments 20X, 3Kb PE 24X, 8Kb PE 6X) using a genome size estimate of 35Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche). This draft assembly was referred to as E_monterogeii_LV88_1.0.3. For the E_monterogeii_LV88_1.0 draft assembly 947 scaffold gaps were closed with Illumina read mapping and local assembly. Next error correction was done by aligning Illumina reads to correct insertion and deletion errors (4790). Finally, 33 contaminating contigs were removed and the scaffolds were arranged into chromosomes. This assembly version E_monterogeii_LV88_1.0.3 is made up of a total of 2558 scaffolds with an N50 scaffold length of over 697kb (N50 contig length was 33kb). The assembly spans 32Mb.

This work was supported by NIH grant AI29646 to SMB and by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW, Director of The Genome Institute at Washington University.

For questions regarding this E_monterogeii_LV88_1.0.3 assembly please contact Dr. Wes Warren, Washington University School of Medicine (wwarren@genome.wustl.edu). Downloads of the sequence data are available via the TriTrypDB genome browser server. Funding for the sequence characterization of the Endotrypanum monterogeii LV88 genome was provided by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Credits:
Strain - Drs. Michael Chance (Liverpool) and Stephen Beverley (St. Louis).

DNA source - Drs. Stephen Beverley, and Natalia Akopyants, Department of Molecular Microbiology, Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis, MO.

Sequencing - The Genome Institute, Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis, MO.

Sequence assembly - The Genome Institute, Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis, MO.

Chromosomal assembly - Sascha Steinbiss, Sanger Institute

Citation upon use of this assembly in a manuscript:
It is requested that users of this sequence assembly acknowledge Stephen M. Beverley and The Genome Institute, Washington University School of Medicine in any publications that result from use of this sequence assembly.

biosample.project_name: Nectria haematococca mpVI 77-13-4

assembly_info.comments:
URL -- http://www.jgi.doe.gov/nectria
JGI Project ID: 4000374
Available as isolate 9596 from the Fungal Genetics Stock Center (School of Biological Sciences, University of Missouri, Kansas City, Missouri, USA) or as isolate S-2067 from the Fusarium Research Center (Department of Plant Pathology, 216 Buckhout Laboratory, Penn State University, University Park, PA, USA)
Contacts: Hans VanEtten (vanetten@Ag.arizona.edu)
Igor Grigoriev (ivgrigoriev@lbl.gov)
Annotation done by JGI-PGF and the Nectria Consortium.
History of Nectria haematococca MPVI isolate 77-13-4: This is an isolate that originated from the PhD dissertation work of Harold Kistler 1983 "Phytoalexin metabolism and implications for phytoalexin tolerance and virulence in two plant pathogenic fungi". Cornell University. It is isolated from a tetrad of a third-generation cross from two field isolates in which one parent, T-2, was isolated from infected pea in upstate NY (Genesee Valley) by Gary Harmon. The other parent, T-219, came from the Penn State collection (isolate S-544) and was isolated from the soil from a potato field in Pennsylvania. The Cross 77 was reported in two publications in 1984 (Kistler, H.C. and H.D. VanEtten. 1984. Journal of General Microbiology 130:2595-2603; Kistler, H. C., VanEtten, H. D. 1984. Journal of General Microbiology 130:2605-13.) but isolate 77-13-4 was not specifically mentioned. This isolate is specifically mentioned and shown to have a supernumerary chromosome in the following publication: Wasmann, C. C. and H. D. VanEtten. 1996. Molecular Plant-Microbe Interactions 9: 793-803.
DNA isolation was done as reported in Temporini ED, VanEtten HD (2002) Curr Genet 41: 107-114.
Taxonomy: Nectria haematococca is commonly referred to by its asexual name Fusarium solani and is a member of a monophyletic clade that includes over 50 phylogenetic species known as the "Fusarium solani species complex". Members of the Fusarium solani species complex that cause infections in both humans and plants are common in the environment. The most extensively studied species of the F. solani complex is "mating population" (MP) VI of N. haematococca (also called Haematonectria haematococca). The term "mating population" defines a group of isolates that are sexually fertile with one another, indicating that they are a biological species.
The assembly is ordered and orientated on the optical map. A significant number of smaller scaffolds (7.7% of the total sequence) is not mapped to chromosomes.
(http://www.genome.gov/page.cfm?pageID=10506376)

Assembly Method: Jazz + optical map
Assembly Name: v2.0
Genome Coverage: 8.2x
Sequencing Technology: Sanger

assembly_info.comments:
Background: The Leishmania aethiopica strain L147 (WHO strain identifier MHOM/ET/1972/L100) was obtained from Charles Jaffe (Israel). This parasite was isolated in Ethiopia in Wollega Province near to a place called Nekempti. It was obtained from a relapsing skin lesion of a 9-year old male, who was a classical case of diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL); his skin test was negative (as is typical for DCL). The excreted factor (EF) sub-serotype is B1. Other designations for Strain LRC-L147 are LV24 (Liverpool School of Trop. Med. collection number). (Strain information provided by Lee Schnur, Israel). PCR tests using primers recognizing both LRV1 and LRV2 were negative. Genomic DNA was prepared by CsCl/Ethidium bromide density gradient centrifugation to minimize the amount of kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA, and was provided by Drs. Natalia Akopyants and Stephen Beverley, Washington University School of Medicine. The input sequence coverage of Illumina instrument fragment reads was 110X, while the final assembled coverage was 220X (fragments, 3 and 8kb) using a genome size estimate of 35Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the ALLPATHS software (Broad Institute). This draft assembly is referred to as Leishmania aethiopica L147 2.0.3. This version has been cleaned of contaminating contigs, and the scaffolds were arranged into chromosomes. The assembly is made up of a total of 36 scaffolds with an N50 scaffold length of over 1.0Mb (N50 contig length was 38.3kb). The assembly spans 31Mb.
This work was supported by NIH grant AI29646 to SMB and by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW, Director of The Genome Institute at Washington University.
For questions regarding this Leishmania aethiopica L147 2.0.3 assembly please contact Dr. Wesley Warren, Washington University School of Medicine (wwarren@genome.wustl.edu). Downloads of the sequence data are available via the TriTrypDB genome browser server. Funding for the sequence characterization of the Leishmania aethiopica L147 genome was provided by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Source DNA can be obtained by mailing: Stephen M. Beverley, Ph.D. Marvin A. Brennecke Professor and Head of Molecular Microbiology Department of Molecular Microbiology Campus Box 8230 Washington University School of Medicine 660 S. Euclid Ave. St. Louis, MO 63110 USA

assembly_info.comments:
Background:
The Leishmania brazilensis M2903 strain was isolated in 1975 from a cutaneous lesion of a man who contracted the infection in a forested area of Serra dos Carajas, Para State, Brazil (J. Shaw, personal communication; cited in Balanco et al, Parasitology (1998) 116: 103-113).
The WHO strain designation is MHOM/BR/75/M2903. Dr. J. Shaw kindly made this strain available for sequencing, with the assistance of Diane McMahon-Pratt (Yale School of Public Health).
RT-PCR typing with several primer sets shows that this line lacks detectable levels of LRV1 virus. This strain can be readily manipulated genetically and possesses a potent RNAi activity. (Lye, L-F., K. L. Owens, H. Shi, S.M.F. Murta, A.C. Vieira, S.J. Turco, C. Tschudi, E. Ullu, and S.M. Beverley (2010), Retention and loss of RNA interference pathways in Trypanosomatid protozoans, PLoS Pathogens 6: e1001161. PMCID: PMC2965760). It is infective in various animal models according to the literature and in work from the Beverley laboratory.
Genomic DNA was made by CsCl/Ethidium bromide density gradient centrifugation to minimize the amount of kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA.

Next-generation sequences on the 454 instruments were produced for a draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of 454 instrument reads was approx. 71X (Fragments 22X, 3Kb PE 28X, 8Kb PE 17X) using a genome size estimate of 35Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454). This draft assembly was referred to as L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.6. The L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.1 was manually edited to yield version L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.2. In the L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.3 assembly 740 scaffold gaps were closed with Illumina read mapping and local assembly. Assembly error correction was done by aligning Illumina reads to correct insertion and deletion errors (2364). Finally, 34 contaminating contigs were removed and the scaffolds were arranged into chromosomes to yield this L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.6. This version L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.6 is made up of a total of 36 scaffolds with an N50 scaffold length of over 1.23Mb (N50 contig length is 63.7kb). The assembly spans 34.8Mb.

This work was supported by NIH grants AI29646 and AI 31078 to SMB and by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW, Director of The Genome Institute at Washington University.

For questions regarding this L_brazilensis_M2903_1.0.6 assembly please contact Dr. Wes Warren, Washington University School of Medicine (wwarren@genome.wustl.edu). Downloads of the sequence data are available via the TriTrypDB genome browser server. Funding for the sequence characterization of the Leishmania brazilensis M2903 genome was provided by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), National Institutes of Health (NIH).

bioprojects.title: Genome of Indian Leishmania donovani Ld BHU 1220

description.comment: During the year 1998-2000, resistance to the widely used antimonial drug sodium antimony gluconate (SAG) had reached alarming heights in India. At this time we had cultivated many isolates collected from the eastern region of India. The diagnostic criteria for Visceral Leishmaniasis (VL) were the presence of LD bodies (Leishman Donovan) in splenic aspirations performed and graded as per standard criteria. Isolate 2001, isolated on 01.02.2000, from Balia, Uttar Pradesh, responded to SAG therapy. Splenic aspirates were collected and adapted to culture. Assay for in vitro drug sensitivity to sodium antimony gluconate (SAG) was done. The virulence and level of susceptibility or resistance of these isolates was also confirmed in vivo, by infection in experimental animals. Species identity of these promastigotes was confirmed to be similar to the donovani in the sequence based RFLP of their single-copy protein-coding gene, N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate transferase.

owner.name: Washington University School of Medicine, Genome Sequencing Center

assembly_info.comments:
Leishmania major SD 75.1 is a strain of Leishmania, a genus of Trypanosomatid protozoa. It is associated with zoonotic cutaneous leishmaniasis, and it is spread through sandflies. Their primary hosts are vertebrates; Leishmania commonly infects canids, rodents, and humans. Leishmania currently affects 12 million people in 88 countries.

The assembly consists of 454 fragment reads (22X), three kilobase paired end reads (21X), and eight kilobase paired end reads (9X). The reads were assembled with Newbler, and then the assembly was manually improved. A contig N50 of 89K, and a scaffold N50 of 1020K was achieved.

Pathogenomics of Trypanosomatid Parasites
NHGRI Large Scale Sequencing Program for Organismal Sequencing

assembly_info.comments:
Background:
The Leishmania panamensis strain L13 (WHO strain identifier MHOM/COL/81/L13) was obtained from Dr. Nancy Saravia, CIDEIM, Cali, Colombia. This isolate was obtained from a human mucosal lesion from Colombia (Choco, Tado).

Genomic DNA was prepared by CsCl/Ethidium bromide density gradient centrifugation to minimize the amount of kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA, and was provided by Drs. Natalia Akopyants and Stephen Beverley, Washington University School of Medicine.

Total sequence coverage of Illumina instrument reads was 165X (300-500bp inserts 65X, 3Kb PE 99X) using a genome size estimate of 35Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the SOAPdenovo software (BGI). This first draft assembly was referred to as L.panamensis L13_1.3. In the L.panamensis L13_1.3 assembly 9343 scaffold gaps were closed with Illumina read mapping and local assembly. No contaminating contigs were removed to yield version L.panamensis L13_1.3.1. The L.panamensis L13_1.3.1. assembly is made up of a total of 1245 scaffolds with an N50 scaffold length of over 156kb (N50 contig length was 22.5 kb). The assembly spans 31.1Mb.

This work was supported by NIH grant AI29646 to SMB and by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW, Director of The Genome Institute at Washington University.

For questions regarding this L.panamensis L13_1.3.1 assembly please contact Dr. Wesley Warren, Washington University School of Medicine (wwarren@genome.wustl.edu). Downloads of the sequence data are available via the TriTrypDB genome browser server. Funding for the sequence characterization of the Leishmania panamensis L13 genome was provided by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), National Institutes of Health (NIH).

assembly_info.comments:
Background: Leishmania sp. MAR, or Martinique, LEM2494 (MHOM/MQ/92/MAR1) was obtained from Professeurs Jean-Pierre Dedet and Patrick Bastien, University Montepellier, France. This parasite was isolated from a skin lesion of a human patient exhibiting diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis and infected with HIV. H. Noyes, F. Pratlong, M. Chance, J. Ellis, G. Lanotte & J-P. Dedet (2002), A previously unclassified trypanosomatid responsible for human cutaneous lesions in Martinique (French West Indies) is the most divergent member of the genus Leishmania, Parasitology (2002), 124, 17-24; J-P. Dedet, B. Roche, F. Pratlong, D. Cales-Quist, J. Jouannelle, J.C. Benichou & M. Huerre (1995), Diffuse cutaneous infection caused by a presumed monoxenous trypanosomatid in a patient infected with HIV, Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene 89:644-646. Genomic DNA was prepared from nuclei isolated from parasites lysed using 0.5% NP-40, to minimize the amount of kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA, and was provided by Drs. Deborah E Dobson and Stephen M. Beverley, Washington University School of Medicine. Total sequence coverage of Illumina instrument reads was 187X (fragments, 3 and 8kb) using a genome size estimate of 35Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the ALLPATHS software (Broad Institute). This draft assembly was referred to as Leishmania sp. MAR LEM2494 1.0.3. This version has been gap filled and cleaned of contaminating contigs. The assembly is made up of a total of 337 scaffolds with an N50 scaffold length of over 489kb (N50 contig length was 147kb). The assembly spans 30.5Mb. This work was supported by NIH grant AI29646 to SMB and by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW, Director of The Genome Institute at Washington University. For questions regarding this Leishmania sp. MAR LEM2494 1.0.2 assembly please contact Dr. Wesley Warren, Washington University School of Medicine (wwarren@genome.wustl.edu). Downloads of the sequence data are available via the TriTrypDB genome browser server. Funding for the sequence characterization of the Leishmania MAR LEM2494 genome was provided by the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), National Institutes of Health (NIH).

assembly_info.comments:
URL -- http://www.jgi.doe.gov

Source DNA available from Brett M. Tyler (bmtyler@vt.edu)
Contacts: Brett M. Tyler (bmtyler@vt.edu)
Igor Grigoriev (ivgrigoriev@lbl.gov)
This genome was very difficult to improve due to the very high repeat content which was evident also on the clone level. To improve the genome, we (i) sequenced P. sojae BAC End libraries and reassembled the genome using Arachne; (ii) finished scaffolds using primer walks from subclones, transposon hopping of subclones, followed by direct BAC and fosmid sequencing; (iii) removed redundant scaffolds and linked the rest using a map generated with Illumina genotyping.

bioprojects.title: The genome sequence of the popular hexose transport deficient Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain EBY.VW4000 reveals LoxP/Cre-induced translocations and gene loss.

attributes.name: genotype
attributes.value: MATa leu2-3,112 ura3-52 trp1-289 his3-delta1 MAL2-8c SUC2 hxt13delta::loxP hxt15delta::loxP hxt16delta::loxP hxt14delta::loxP hxt12delta::loxP hxt9delta::loxP hxt11delta::loxP hxt10delta::loxP hxt8delta::loxP hxt514delta::loxP hxt2delta::loxP hxt367delta::loxP gal2delta::(ura3/FOA) stl1delta::loxP agt1delta::loxP mph2(ydl247w)delta::loxP mph3(yjr160c)delta::loxP

description.comment: Saccharomyces cerevisiae harbours a large group of tightly controlled transporters with different characteristics for glucose uptake. A milestone in the characterization of S. cerevisiae s transporters was the construction of EBY.VW4000, a strain devoid of glucose import. Since its construction, EBY.VW4000 has become a widely used platform for the discovery and characterization of transporters from a wide range of organisms. To abolish glucose uptake, 21 genes were knocked-out across 16 successive deletion rounds with the LoxPCre system. While these genetic approaches notoriously trigger genome alterations, the genome of EBY.VW4000 has hitherto never been characterized. Based on a combination of whole genome sequencing, karyotyping and molecular confirmation, the present study reveals that the construction of EBY.VW4000 resulted in many gene losses and chromosomal rearrangements. Recombinations between the LoxP scars has led to the assembly of four neo-chromosomes, the truncation of two chromosomes and the loss of two telomeric regions. Karyotyping of the EBY.VW400 lineage retraced the current chromosomal architecture to four translocations events that occurred between the 6th and the 12th rounds of deletion/marker recycling. The presented data provide support for further targeted genetic modifications of EBY.VW4000. Furthermore, the present study identified that sporulation and spore germination are severely impaired in EBY.VW4000.

description.comment: The tetraploid Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain GSY2239 was derived from the industrial brewing strain GSY161 (Wyeast Laboratories strain 1833; probable origin Duvel Moortgat Brewery, Belgium). GSY161 was sporulated and diploid progeny were isolated using tetrad microdissection. A single diploid spore was self-mated to form tetraploid strain GSY2167. An additional round of meiosis and self-mating was performed on isolate GSY2167 to minimize heterozygosity, yielding isolate GSY2239.

owner.name: Washington University School of Medicine, Genome Sequencing Center

assembly_info.comments:
S. cerevisiae strain CBS7960 was isolated from in a factory in Sao Paulo, Brazil, which produces ethanol from cane-sugar syrup. It is in the industrial yeast DBVPG collection in Perugia, Italy as DBVPG7960, or the strain may be obtained from Dr. Justin Fay, Washington University School of Medicine. DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho- derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described.

454 (and/or 3730) instruments were used to produce a draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genome was 7.3X (3730 9.69X) using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Pcap software.

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.

assembly_info.comments:
S. cerevisiae strain CLIB382 was isolated from super-attenuated beer prepared in an Irish brewery pre-1952. The strain exists in several stock culture collections. It is in the CBS collection as CBS1782, in the DBVPG collection as DBVPG6175, in the NCYC collection as NCYC361, and in the NRRL collection as NRRL YB4238. The strain also may be obtained from Dr. Justin Fay, Washington University School of Medicine. DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho- derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described. 454 instruments were used to produce a survey coverage draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genome was 5.96X using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454).

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.

bioprojects.title: Saccharomyces cerevisiae PW5 genome sequencing
Saccharomyces cerevisiae Strain Project

assembly_info.comments:
S. cerevisiae strain PW5 was isolated from Raphia palm wine in Aba, Abia state, Nigeria in 2002. The strain may be obtained from Dr. Justin Fay, Washington University School of Medicine. DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho- derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described. 454 instruments were used to produce a high coverage draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genome was 16.10X using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb.

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.

DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho- derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described. 454 (and/or 3730) instruments were used to produce a survey coverage draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genome was 25.4X using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454).

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.

description.title: Generic sample from Saccharomyces cerevisiae YPS163

assembly_info.comments:
Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain YPS163 was isolated from an oak tree in Pennsylvania, USA in 1999. The strain may be obtained from Dr. Justin Fay, Washington University School of Medicine. DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho-derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described. 454 (and/or 3730) instruments were used to produce a high coverage draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genome was
12.9X using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454).

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.

description.title: Generic sample from Saccharomyces kudriavzevii FM1056

assembly_info.comments:
Reference guided assembly based on Saccharomyces kudriavzevii IFO1802 in INSD accession number AACI00000000.

Contigs 9001, 9002, 9004, and 9080 are present only in Gal+ strains. They are syntenic to the GAL pseudogenes and surrounding regions. Illumina reads from all strains were allowed to assemble to either the functional or pseudogene alleles in these regions, whereas all other contigs had only IFO1802 as the reference strain. For each strain, only one allele is present and leads to significant coverage. See the full methods in Hittinger et al. 2010 (PMID:20164837) for details.

bioprojects.title: Chromosomal copy number variation in Saccharomyces pastorianus: evidence for extensive genome dynamics in industrial lager brewing strains.

description.comment: S. pastorianus is a hybrid of S. cerevisiae and a species closely related to S. bayanus. This result was further refined by the recent discovery and genome analysis of S. eubayanus, whose genome sequence shows a 99.5% identity with that of the non-cerevisiae part of the S. pastorianus genome. Originally isolated from oak trees in Nothofagus (Southern beech) forests and stromata of Cyttaria hariotii (an ascomycetous parasite of Nothofagus spp.) in Patagonia, S. eubayanus has recently also been isolated in North America and Asia . Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the Tibetan population of the S. eubayanus lineage was more closely related with S. pastorianus than the type strain CBS12357 (PYCC 6148) from Patagonia. The strain CBS1483 has been deposited first to the CBS -KNAW biodiversity Centre in July 1927 for the first time.

assembly_info.comments:
Trypanosoma brucei chromosomes 9 to 11 were isolated and then sequenced by the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute, using a whole chromosome shotgun approach. The sequences are therefore, likely to represent a 'mosaic' assembly of both chromosomal homologs. Details of Trypanosoma sequencing at the Sanger Institute are available on the World Wide Web. (URL, http://www.sanger.ac.uk/Projects/T_brucei/) and via the GeneDB database (www.genedb.org).
Predicted protein coding regions (>30 codons) were manually revised in the light of similarity data, domain information and orthology to Leishmania major and Trypanosoma cruzi. Gene products were assigned putative functions based on similarity with experimentally characterized gene products or the presence of predicted protein domains. Products were labelled either 'hypothetical protein', or 'hypothetical protein, conserved' when showing significant similarity with proteins or domains of unknown function from other organisms. Short predicted coding sequences (less than 150 codons) with no additional evidence of coding potential were labeled 'hypothetical protein, unlikely'.

biosample.isolation_source: 55 year old mail patient in chronic syptomatic stage of disease

owner.name: Washington University School of Medicine, The Genome Institute

assembly_info.comments:
Background:

The Trypanosome cruzi JR strain cl4 was obtained from Dr. Gregory Buck, Center for the Study of Biological Complexity, Microbiology and Immunology, Virginia Commonwealth University. This strain, a representative of the TcI lineage of T. cruzi (Hamilton et al., 2011), was isolated from a male patient, age 55, in chronic symptomatic stage of disease in Anzoategui, Venezuela by Dr. Hernan Carrasco and his colleagues at the Universidad Central de Venezuela (Lewis et al., 2009). A clonal derivative was prepared from epimastigote culture by plating on blood agar plates (M. Lewis) and used for sequencing.
Genomic DNA was depleted for kinetoplast (mitochondrial) DNA (kDNA), which represents up to 30-50% of the total DNA in the cell, by Dr. Andrey Matveyev. In brief, total DNA was extracted from cultured late log phase T. cruzi JR epimastigote forms and submitted to low voltage electrophoresis in 0.8% low melting agarose. The gDNA-containing agarose blocks were excised from the gel, leaving the kDNA networks intact in the gel. Purified gDNA was recovered from the agarose blocks after digestion using Beta-agarase I.

The gDNA was fragmented and sequenced using the Roche 454 FLX Titanium technology and a draft assembly was produced. Total sequence coverage from the Roche 454 technology was approximately 50X (fragments @ 22X, 3 Kb paired end (PE) @20X, 8 Kb PE @ 6.5X) using a genome size estimate of 40 Mbp. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454). This first draft assembly was referred to as T._cruzi_JR cl4-1.1. The T._cruzi_JR cl4-1.1 version was manually edited to create version T._cruzi_JR cl4-1.1.1. In the T._cruzi_JR cl4-1.1.1 assembly 2962 scaffold gaps were closed with Illumina read mapping and local assembly. Assembly error correction was done by aligning Illumina reads to correct insertion and deletion errors (6500). Finally, 22 contaminating contigs were removed to yield version T._cruzi_JR cl4-1.1.4. The T._cruzi_JR cl4-1.1.4 assembly is made up of a total of 18,177 scaffolds with an N50 scaffold length of over 72kb (N50 contig length is 7.1 kb) and assembled size spans 40.5 Mb.

description.comment: Babesia sp. Xinjiang is a large Babesia species of sheep and other small ruminants in the Kashi prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwestern China. This haematoprotozoan parasite belongs to the phylum Apicomplexa and is genetically distinct from other recognized species of Babesia from sheep (e.g., B. motasi, B. ovis and B. crassa) and from other host animals. This parasite is non-pathogenic in sheep, but causes classical symptoms of babesiosis, such as fever, anaemia, icterus and haemoglobinuria, in experimentally infected, splenectomized sheep.

bioprojects.title: Elucidation of adaptive evolutionary patterns in an mycotoxigenic emerging pathogen Fusarium proliferatum: Development of the genome sequence of biogeographically diverse isolates

description.comment: Fusarium proliferatum is an emerging pathogen associated with diverse plant hosts and distributed in wide geographic locations. F. proliferatum is recognised as a major mycotoxigenic species among crop pathogenic Fusariums. The aim of this study is to further our understanding of the genetic diversity, biological variability including fumonisin production, and the genomic architecture in F. proliferatum. We have used collection of 52 isolates representing different hosts and geographic locations. The genome sequence data has been generated for four distinctive isolates. The overall goal is to gain insights into the adaptive evolutionary patterns of this pathogen with reference to its biogeographic diversity.

assembly_info.comments:
The Malaria Host-Pathogen Interaction Center (MaHPIC) is a transdisciplinary malaria systems biology research program supported by an NIH/NIAID contract (# HHSN272201200031C; see http://www.systemsbiology.emory.edu). The MaHPIC generates many data types (e.g., genomic, clinical, hematological, parasitological, metabolomics, functional genomics, lipidomics, proteomics, immune response) and mathematical models, to iteratively test and develop hypotheses related to the complex host-parasite dynamics in the course of malaria in non-human primates, and metabolomics data via collaborations with investigators conducting clinical studies in malaria endemic countries, with the overarching goal of better understanding human disease, pathogenesis, and immunity. Curation and maintenance of all data and metadata are the responsibility of the MaHPIC. To access other publicly available MaHPIC results, including clinical and -omics results from MaHPIC experiments, visit http://plasmodb.org/plasmo/mahpic.jsp
Scaffold naming is based on the length of each scaffold in order of shortest to longest.

This is a PacBio-based assembly that was corrected using Illumina HiC. Contigs in scaffolds are connected by gaps represented by runs of 100 N's. PacBio reads belonging to this assembly came from SRA runs SRR5413213- SRR5413218. Illumina HiC reads were deposited in SRA accession SRR5413221. Scaffold naming is based on the length of each scaffold in order of shortest to longest.
The VEuPathDB Bioinformatics Resource Center (www.veupathdb.org) may also have contributed to the annotation of this genome. Annotation and related data can be viewed and updated at http://veupathdb.org and inquiries can be sent to help@veupathdb.org.

bioprojects.title: Saccharomyces kudriavzevii CR85

description.comment: The ability of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to convert glucose, even in the presence of oxygen, via glycolysis and the fermentative pathway to ethanol has played an important role in its domestication. Despite the extensive knowledge on these pathways in S. cerevisiae, relatively little is known about these pathways in other industrially-relevant Saccharomyces yeast species. In this study we explore the diversity of the glycolytic and fermentative pathways within the Saccharomyces genus using S. cerevisiae, S. kudriavzevii and S. eubayanus as paradigms. Sequencing data revealed a highly conserved genetic makeup of the glycolytic and fermentative pathways in the three species in terms of number of paralogous genes. Although promoter regions were less conserved between the three species as compared to coding sequences, binding sites for Rap1, Gcr1 and Abf1, main transcriptional regulators of glycolytic and fermentative genes, were highly conserved. Transcriptome profiling of these three strains grown in aerobic batch cultivation in chemically defined medium with glucose as carbon source, revealed a remarkably similar expression of the glycolytic and fermentative genes across species, and the conserved classification of genes into major and minor paralogs. Furthermore, transplantation of the promoters of major paralogs of S. kudriavzevii and S. eubayanus into S. cerevisiae demonstrated not only the transferability of these promoters, but also the similarity of their strength and response to various environmental stimuli. The relatively low homology of S. kudriavzevii and S. eubayanus promoters to their S. cerevisiae relatives makes them very attractive alternatives for strain construction in S. cerevisiae, thereby expanding S. cerevisiae molecular toolbox.

description.title: Pathogen: clinical or host-associated sample from Trichophyton benhamiae CBS 112371

assembly_info.comments: This is a reannotation of WGS genome ABSU00000000 based on RNA-seq reads and automatic gene annotation, followed by manual curation. RNA-seq reads were mapped to the genome and only those with enough coverage were included. Gene transcripts and intron locations were obtained using cufflinks v. 2.2.1. Transcripts were translated into potential amino-acid sequences using transeq from EMBOSS v. 6.5.7 and mapped to the proteomes of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Aspergillus nidulans with glsearch36, from FASTA alignment tools v. 3.6 to identify coding phase and CDS location within transcripts. Based on the alignment quality and on the presence of start and stop codons near alignment extremities (+/- 10 amino acids), a set of predicted CDS was gathered and converted into gene annotations using intron locations previously given by cufflinks. These annotations were used as a training set to build a gene model with augustus v. 3.0.2.

description.comment: Comparative analyses have indicated that the mitochondrion of the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) likely possessed all the key core structures and functions that are widely conserved throughout the domain Eucarya. Traditionally, such studies have largely focused on multicellular eukaryotes: animals, fungi and plants; relatively few mitochondrial proteomes from protists (single-celled eukaryotes) have been determined. To gauge the full extent of mitochondrial structural and functional complexity, and to identify potential evolutionatry trends in mitochondrial proteomes, deeper detailed explorations of diverse mitochondrial proteomes are required. A key group is the jakobids, a clade of protists belonging to the deeply-diverging eukaryotic supergroup Discoba, distinguished by having the most gene-rich and most bacteria-like mitochondrial genomes discovered to date. In this study, we assembled the draft nuclear genome sequence for the jakobid Andalucia godoyi and used a comprehensive in silico approach to infer the nucleus-encoded portion of the mitochondrial proteome of this protist, identifying 857 candidate mitochondrial proteins. Our results demonstrate that the A. godoyi mitochondrial proteome has a complexity that parallels that of other eukaryotes, while exhibiting a number of ancestral features that have been lost particularly in opisthokont (animal and fungal) mitochondria. Notably, we find no evidence that the A. godoyi nuclear genome has or had a gene encoding a single-subunit, T3/T7 bacteriophage-like RNA polymerase that functions as the mitochondrial transcriptase in all eukaryotes except the jakobids.

bioprojects.title: Aspergillus niger strain:RAF106 Genome sequencing and assembly

description.comment: Aspergillus niger has been generally regarded as a safe material by FDA and developed in some scaled-up processes to produce different enzymes. Aspergillus niger RAF106 could convert ester-catechins into non-ester-catechin and gallic acid, and also degrade non-ester-catechin and gallic acid into compounds with smaller molecular weight, which might improve the bioavailabilities and bioactivities of ester-catechins. However, there is no genomic information about Aspergillus niger which could mediate the biotransformation of catechins. Thus we sequenced the complete genome of A. niger RAF106 in order to analyze the differences between A. niger RAF106 and other Aspergillus niger, and illustrate the potential mechanisms on the biotransformation of catechins mediated A. niger RAF106.

assembly_info.comments:

The strain is in the NRRL collection or it may be obtained from Dr. Justin Fay, Washington University School of Medicine. DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho-derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described. 454 (and/or 3730) instruments were used to produce a survey coverage draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genome was
27.8X using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454).

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907 to RKW.

bioprojects.title: Nanopore sequencing and comparative genome analysis confirm lager-brewing yeasts originated from a single hybridization

description.comment: The lager brewing yeast S. pastorianus is a hybrid between S. cerevisiae and S. eubayanus with extensive chromosome aneuploidy. S. pastorianus is subdivided into Group 1 and Group 2 strains: Group 2 strains have higher copy number and a larger degree of heterozygosity for S. cerevisiae chromosomes. As a result, Group 2 strains were hypothesized to have emerged from a hybridization event distinct from Group 1 strains. Current genome assemblies of S. pastorianus strains are incomplete and highly fragmented, limiting our ability to investigate their evolutionary history. To fill this gap, we generated a chromosome-level genome assembly of the S. pastorianus strain CBS 1483 using MinION sequencing and analysed the newly assembled subtelomeric regions and chromosome heterozygosity. To analyse the evolutionary history of S. pastorianus strains, we developed Alpaca: a method to compute sequence similarity between genomes without assuming linear evolution. Alpaca revealed high similarities between the S. cerevisiae subgenomes of Group 1 and 2 strains, and marked differences from sequenced S. cerevisiae strains. Our findings suggest that Group 1 and Group 2 strains originated from a single hybridization involving a heterozygous S. cerevisiae strain, followed by loss of S. cerevisiae genome content in Group 1 strains. The clear differences between both groups may originate from dissemination from few initial isolates. Furthermore, Alpaca provides a computationally inexpensive method to analyse evolutionary relationships while considering non-linear evolution such as horizontal gene transfer and sexual reproduction, providing a complementary viewpoint beyond traditional phylogenetic approaches.

description.comment: S. pastorianus is a hybrid of S. cerevisiae and a species closely related to S. bayanus. This result was further refined by the recent discovery and genome analysis of S. eubayanus, whose genome sequence shows a 99.5% identity with that of the non-cerevisiae part of the S. pastorianus genome. Originally isolated from oak trees in Nothofagus (Southern beech) forests and stromata of Cyttaria hariotii (an ascomycetous parasite of Nothofagus spp.) in Patagonia, S. eubayanus has recently also been isolated in North America and Asia . Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the Tibetan population of the S. eubayanus lineage was more closely related with S. pastorianus than the type strain CBS12357 (PYCC 6148) from Patagonia. The strain CBS1483 has been deposited first to the CBS -KNAW biodiversity Centre in July 1927 for the first time.

description.comment: Genome of T. cruzi CL, a highly virulent mammal-infective trypanosome. This strain was isolated in Brazil in 1963 from its insect vector Triatoma infestans.
description.title: Trypanosoma cruzi CL genome

assembly_info.comments: This diploid assembly contains pseudo-haplotypes from the Trypanosoma cruzi CL strain. The genome assembly was created using the T. cruzi CL Brener assembly from TriTrypDB v.24 as a reference. Reads were mapped to the entire T. cruzi CL Brener genome with BWA, and reads aligning to each haplotype were extracted for use in individual haplotype assembly runs (run performed in Newbler, with no reference assembly provided during assembly process). Contigs <500 bp in length were removed from the final assemblies. The primary haplotype sequences (Esmeraldo-like) are MKQG01000001-MKQG01002387. The alternative haplotype sequences (non-Esmeraldo-like) are MKQG01002388-MKQG01004677. Sequences that were unable to be distinguished between the haplotypes are MKQG01004678-MKQG01007764.

description.comment: About Yarrowia lipolytica str. CLIB89 (W29) Yarrowia is a fungal genus in the family Dipodascaceae. For a while the genus was monotypic, containing the single species Yarrowia lipolytica, a yeast that can use unusual carbon sources, such as hydrocarbons. This has made it of interest for use in industrial microbiology, especially for the production of specialty lipids. Molecular phylogenetics analysis has revealed several other species that have since been added to the genus.

bioprojects.title: Elucidation of adaptive evolutionary patterns in an mycotoxigenic emerging pathogen Fusarium proliferatum: Development of the genome sequence of biogeographically diverse isolates

description.comment: Fusarium proliferatum is an emerging pathogen associated with diverse plant hosts and distributed in wide geographic locations. F. proliferatum is recognised as a major mycotoxigenic species among crop pathogenic Fusariums. The aim of this study is to further our understanding of the genetic diversity, biological variability including fumonisin production, and the genomic architecture in F. proliferatum. We have used collection of 52 isolates representing different hosts and geographic locations. The genome sequence data has been generated for four distinctive isolates. The overall goal is to gain insights into the adaptive evolutionary patterns of this pathogen with reference to its biogeographic diversity.

assembly_info.comments: This organism is a lab generated hybrid. Long and short read sequencing technologies were used to get better coverage of the genome. After assembling the genome, BLAST was used to try and separate out the sequences based on the parental organisms (Ogataea polymorpha and Ogataea parapolymorpha). As such the contigs are named either Opar or Opoly for polymorpha or parapolymorpha respectively, and thus this genome represents the complete pool of DNA present in this hybrid organism.#

bioprojects.title: Saccharomyces cerevisiae IL-01 genome sequencing
Saccharomyces cerevisiae Strain Project

owner.name: Washington University School of Medicine, Genome Sequencing Center

assembly_info.comments:
S. cerevisiae strain IL-01 was isolated from a soil sample in Cahokia, Illinois in 2003. The strain may be obtained from Dr. Justin Fay, Washington University School of Medicine. DNA was prepared in the laboratory of Dr. Justin Fay by Juyoung Huh. All sequencing was performed using the rho-derivatives of monosporic clones or haploid clones from the strains described. 454 instruments were used to produced a survey coverage draft assembly. Total sequence coverage of the genomewas
8.47X using a genome size estimate of 14-16 Mb. The combined sequence reads were assembled using the Newbler software (Roche 454).

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.
assembly_info.submitter: Genome Sequencing Center (GSC) at Washington University (WashU) School of Medicine

This work was supported by NIH-NHGRI grant 5U54HG00307907.

Starmer from a fir flux in the Catalina Mountains, Southern AZ, USA. K. kurtzmanii differs from its phenotypically similar sibling species Komagataella pastoris, Komagataella pseudopastoris, Komagataella phaffii, Komagataella populi and Komagataella ulmi by absence of growth at 35 C and inability to assimilate trehalose.

bioprojects.title: Fusarium avenaceum strain:WV21P1A Genome sequencing and assembly

attributes.name: isolation_source
attributes.value: European pear (Pyrus communis L.) Dawn with brown, circular, watery, and sunken lesions was observed in cold storage

description.comment: Fusarium avenaceum has a large host range and has been reported to cause disease on over 80 genera of plants. A F. avenaceum isolate was obtained in December 2021 from a decaying European pear (Pyrus communis L.) Dawn with brown, circular, watery, and sunken lesions that was in cold storage at the USDA Appalachian Fruit Research Station located in Kearneysville, West Virginia. Koch's postulates were conducted using six Bartlett pear fruits that were wound-inoculated with mycelial plugs of the fungus. Brown, circular, watery, and sunken lesions developed within 48 hours after inoculation and incubation at 25 C, while PDA plug inoculated fruit were symptomless. The fungus was reisolated from infected pears and was morphologically identical to the original isolate. Identity of the isolate was confirmed through DNA extraction followed by amplification and sequencing of the ITS and TEF1 gene region. The ITS amplicon (OP007197) matched multiple Fusarium spp. with 100% identity and 100% query coverage including F. avanaceum (KY910897 and KU936793). The TEF1 amplicon (OP007198) showed 98-99% identity and 98-100% query coverage with F. avenaceum isolates KM189442 and MK512754. F. avenaceum can produce mycotoxins, which is a concern for the fruit processing industry. This is the first report of F. avenaceum causing postharvest decay of European pear in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States.
description.title: Fusarium avenaceum isolated from a post-harvest rotted pear

attributes.name: project_name
attributes.value: Bacteria that persist in hospitals can contribute to the establishment of the microbiome in newborns and the spread of hospital-acquired diseases. Yet we know little about microbial communities in hospitals, or about the extent to which persistent vs. recently immigrated bacterial strains establish in the gastrointestinal tracts of hospitalized individuals.</p><p>In combination with BioProject PRJNA273761 (10 infants / 55 samples) we analyzed strain-resolved genomes obtained from a total of 202 samples collected over a three-year period from 21 infants hospitalized in the same intensive care unit.</p><p>Strains were rarely shared, consistent with prior analysis of a subset of these data. Enterococcus faecalis and Staphylococcus epidermidis, common gut colonists, exhibit diversity comparable to that of NCBI reference strains, suggesting no recent common ancestor for all populations in this hospital setting. Thus, we infer multiple introduction events for these species. Despite the rarity of shared strains, strains of five species exhibiting a degree of sequence variation consistent with in situ diversification were identified in different infants hospitalized three years apart. Three were also detected in multiple infants in the same year, suggesting that these strains are unusually widely dispersed and persistent in the hospital environment. Persistent strains were not significantly different from non-persistent strains with regards to pathogenicity potential including antibiotic resistance. Notably, non-identical siblings had multiple abundant strains in common, even 30 days after birth and antibiotic administration, suggesting overlapping strain sources and/or genetic selection. Our approach can be used in order to study microbial dynamics in hospitals and provides an important step towards directing health-promoting colonization in hospitalized individuals.

attributes.name: project_name
attributes.value: Wine is a complex beverage, comprised of thousands of metabolites that are produced through the action of yeasts and bacteria in fermenting grape must. To ensure a robust and reliable fermentation, most commercial wines are produced via inoculation with large amounts of the major wine yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. However, there is a growing trend towards the use of uninoculated or “wild” fermentations, in which the yeasts and bacteria that are naturally associated with the vineyard or winery perform the fermentation. The varied metabolic contributions of the numerous non-Saccharomyces species in this microbial community are thought to impart complexity and desirable taste and aroma attributes to wild ferments when compared to their inoculated counterparts.</p><p>In order the map the microflora of spontaneous fermentation, metagenomic techniques were used to characterise and monitor the progression of fungal species in several wild fermentations. Both amplicon-based ITS phylotyping and shotgun metagenomics were used to assess community structure, in addition to the isolation, sequencing and de novo assembly of the first reference genomes for several dominant wine-associated species.

assembly_info.comments: The assembly pEimTen1.1 is based on 41x PacBio data, 10X Genomics Chromium data, and Arima Hi-C data generated by the Darwin Tree of Life Project (https://www.darwintreeoflife.org/). PacBio subreads were assembled with Canu, contigs were deduplicated using Gap5, and the assembly was scaffolded with scaff10x using E. tenella 10x Chromium Illumina reads. This was then broken with break10x and re-scaffolded using SALSA2 and E. tenella Hi-C reads. Juicebox and Tigmint were used to break scaffolds. RaGOO was then used to re-scaffold, using another assembly generated from the same PacBio reads using wtdbg2. The assembly was then polished with Arrow and Pilon, using 10x Chromium Illumina reads. It then underwent manual curation before final polishing with Pilon. Chromosome-scale scaffolds confirmed by the Hi-C data have been named in reverse order of size. Annnotation was initially generated using Companion, with Eimeria tenella strain Houghton as the reference, and the annotations were then manually curated by Uli Bohme.

attributes.name: project_name
attributes.value: Premature infants are highly vulnerable to aberrant gastrointestinal tract colonization, a process that may lead to diseases like necrotizing enterocolitis. This study compares microbial communities of 10 co-hospitalized infants, five of which had a diagnosis of necrotizing enterocolitis. Surprisingly, while potentially pathogenic bacteria of the same species colonized many infants, a genome-resolved analysis revealed that strains colonizing each baby were typically distinct. In particular, no strain was common to all infants that developed necrotizing enterocolitis. The paucity of shared gut colonizers suggests the existence of significant barriers to spread of bacteria among infants. Importantly, we demonstrate that strain-resolved comprehensive community analysis can be accomplished on potentially medically-relevant time scales.

assembly_info.comments: The assembly gsMetZobe1.1 is based on 90x PacBio data, 10X Genomics Chromium data, and Arima2 Hi-C data generated by the Darwin Tree of Life Project (https://www.darwintreeoflife.org/). The assembly process included the following sequence of steps: initial PacBio assembly generation with Hifiasm, retained haplotig separation with purge_dups, and Hi-C based scaffolding with SALSA2. The mitochondrial genome was assembled using MitoHiFi. Finally, the assembly was analysed and manually improved using rapid curation. Chromosome-scale scaffolds confirmed by the Hi-C data have been named in order of size.

attributes.value: Two out of three datasets (the first one already published with Hugerth et al 2015) included in the Baltic Sea reference metagenome assembly. The assembly include herein is a coassembly of all three datasets, complete with annotated genes to facilitate further studies of the Baltic Sea with much less computational effort. The assembly is constructed using 2.6 billion metagenomic reads from 81 water samples, spanning both spatial and temporal dimensions, and contains 6.8 million genes that have been annotated for function and taxonomy. The assembly is useful as a reference, facilitating taxonomic and functional annotation of additional samples by simply mapping their reads against the assembly.

bioprojects.title: Sequencing and comparative genomics of Candida glabrata isolate FFUL887

attributes.name: description
attributes.value: In this work a phenotypic screening over a cohort of clinical Candida glabrata isolates was undertaken leading to the identification of an isolate, named FFUL887, which was recovered from the urinary tract and that was found to be resistant to both fluconazole and voriconazole. To better understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the azole-resistance phenotype of the FFUL887 strain its genome sequence was obtained, annotated and compared with the one of the reference strain CBS138, susceptible to the two above mentioned azoles and having an intestinal origin. Besides providing clues to mechanisms underlying acquisition of azole resistance inside the host, our results also provide insights into the different responses evolved by C. glabrata in the colonization of different niches.

bioprojects.title: Macroevolutionary diversity of traits and genomes in the model yeast genus Saccharomyces

description.comment: The lager brewing yeast S. pastorianus is a hybrid between S. cerevisiae and S. eubayanus with extensive chromosome aneuploidy. S. pastorianus is subdivided into Group 1 and Group 2 strains: Group 2 strains have higher copy number and a larger degree of heterozygosity for S. cerevisiae chromosomes. As a result, Group 2 strains were hypothesized to have emerged from a hybridization event distinct from Group 1 strains. Current genome assemblies of S. pastorianus strains are incomplete and highly fragmented, limiting our ability to investigate their evolutionary history. To fill this gap, we generated a chromosome-level genome assembly of the S. pastorianus strain CBS 1483 using MinION sequencing and analysed the newly assembled subtelomeric regions and chromosome heterozygosity. To analyse the evolutionary history of S. pastorianus strains, we developed Alpaca: a method to compute sequence similarity between genomes without assuming linear evolution. Alpaca revealed high similarities between the S. cerevisiae subgenomes of Group 1 and 2 strains, and marked differences from sequenced S. cerevisiae strains. Our findings suggest that Group 1 and Group 2 strains originated from a single hybridization involving a heterozygous S. cerevisiae strain, followed by loss of S. cerevisiae genome content in Group 1 strains. The clear differences between both groups may originate from dissemination from few initial isolates. Furthermore, Alpaca provides a computationally inexpensive method to analyse evolutionary relationships while considering non-linear evolution such as horizontal gene transfer and sexual reproduction, providing a complementary viewpoint beyond traditional phylogenetic approaches.

bioprojects.title: Comparative genomics between S. cerevisiae and S. kudriavzevii.
Comparative genomics between S. cerevisiae and S. kudriavzevii.

description.comment: The ability of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to convert glucose, even in the presence of oxygen, via glycolysis and the fermentative pathway to ethanol has played an important role in its domestication. Despite the extensive knowledge on these pathways in S. cerevisiae, relatively little is known about these pathways in other industrially-relevant Saccharomyces yeast species. In this study we explore the diversity of the glycolytic and fermentative pathways within the Saccharomyces genus using S. cerevisiae, S. kudriavzevii and S. eubayanus as paradigms. Sequencing data revealed a highly conserved genetic makeup of the glycolytic and fermentative pathways in the three species in terms of number of paralogous genes. Although promoter regions were less conserved between the three species as compared to coding sequences, binding sites for Rap1, Gcr1 and Abf1, main transcriptional regulators of glycolytic and fermentative genes, were highly conserved. Transcriptome profiling of these three strains grown in aerobic batch cultivation in chemically defined medium with glucose as carbon source, revealed a remarkably similar expression of the glycolytic and fermentative genes across species, and the conserved classification of genes into major and minor paralogs. Furthermore, transplantation of the promoters of major paralogs of S. kudriavzevii and S. eubayanus into S. cerevisiae demonstrated not only the transferability of these promoters, but also the similarity of their strength and response to various environmental stimuli. The relatively low homology of S. kudriavzevii and S. eubayanus promoters to their S. cerevisiae relatives makes them very attractive alternatives for strain construction in S. cerevisiae, thereby expanding S. cerevisiae molecular toolbox.

biosample.project_name: DTOL

assembly_info.comments:
The assembly paTetJugo1.1 is based on 37x PacBio data and Arima2 Hi-C data generated by the Darwin Tree of Life Project
(https://www.darwintreeoflife.org/). The assembly process included the following sequence of steps: Tiara 1.0.1 [PMID: 34570171] was run with PacBio HiFi reads. Reads classified as prokaryotic by Tiara were removed and the remaining reads were assembled using hifiasm (0.14-r312) [PMID: 33526886] with default settings. The hifiasm contigs were checked for contaminants using Tiara 1.0.1 and BLAST against NCBI nt and nr databases (May 2021 versions). Mitochondrial contigs (and chloroplast contigs of ucPycProv1) were detected using Tiara. The longest organellar contigs were circularised using circlator minimus2 (1.5.5) [PMID: 26714481]. The remaining copies of organellar contigs were discarded. Deduplication of chromosomal contigs was done using GAP5 (1.2.14-r) [PMID: 20513662]. The assemblies were scaffolded with Hi-C Arima2 data using SALSA2 (October 2019 version). Finally, the primary assembly was analysed and manually improved using rapid curation. Chromosome-scale scaffolds confirmed by the Hi-C data have been named in order of size. Chromosomes 13 and 39 have triploid coverage.?There is evidence for inter-chromosome rearrangement between chromosome 10 and chromosome 17.

attributes.value: Wine is a complex beverage, comprised of thousands of metabolites that are produced through the action of yeasts and bacteria in fermenting grape must. To ensure a robust and reliable fermentation, most commercial wines are produced via inoculation with large amounts of the major wine yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. However, there is a growing trend towards the use of uninoculated or “wild” fermentations, in which the yeasts and bacteria that are naturally associated with the vineyard or winery perform the fermentation. The varied metabolic contributions of the numerous non-Saccharomyces species in this microbial community are thought to impart complexity and desirable taste and aroma attributes to wild ferments when compared to their inoculated counterparts.</p><p>In order the map the microflora of spontaneous fermentation, metagenomic techniques were used to characterise and monitor the progression of fungal species in several wild fermentations. Both amplicon-based ITS phylotyping and shotgun metagenomics were used to assess community structure, in addition to the isolation, sequencing and de novo assembly of the first reference genomes for several dominant wine-associated species.

description.comment: The yeast species Zygosaccharomyces bailii exhibits a remarkable but poorly understood intrinsic resistance to acetic acid and other weak acids used as food preservatives, being the most significant spoilage yeast especially in acidic drinks and food products. Z. bailii may also be explored in Biotechnology as cell factory when the growth substrates or the bioproducts envisaged includes deleterious concentrations of a wide range of weak acids. The sequence and annotation of the genome of the haploid, non-flocculating strain Z. bailii IST302, isolated from a spontaneous fermentation of grape must, is essential to facilitate the use of genetic engineering technology in this species, which is much more susceptible to manipulate genetically and to study the physiology, compared with the 2 strains with the genome sequence currently available: ISA1307 which is indeed a flocculating hybrid strain, derived from Z. bailii and a closely related species and the highly flocculating CLIB213T. Such better performance of strain IST302 will allow a systems-level understanding of the molecular mechanisms of stress tolerance envisaging the rational control of the activity of this highly threatening spoilage yeast, as well as for inspiring and guiding novel biotechnological applications.

attributes.name: project_name
attributes.value:
16S rRNA gene sequences amplified from subjects with eczema and age-matched healthy controls.

Microbes living in and on humans are ten times more numerous than human cells. Culture-based methods have been the primary techniques used to study microbes inhabiting humans however, many species are not successfully grown in culture. The NIH Roadmap for Medical Research Human Microbiome Project (HMP) aims to investigate the microbes in the gastrointestinal tract, oral cavity, skin, vagina, and nares. The goal of the HMP is to comprehensively characterize the human microbiota and analyze its role in human health and disease.

The skin serves not only as a barrier against invading pathogens and moisture loss, but also as a host to microbial communities. The skin of an adult is an approximately 2 square meter surface with a myriad of microenvironments. Atopic dermatitis (AD), more commonly known as eczema, is a common skin disorder that is exacerbated by Staphylococcus aureus colonization. This study aims to investigate the skin microbiota of AD patients at specific timepoints (quiescence, disease flares, and post-treatment) to examine how disease state correlates with changes in the skin microflora.

The 16S small subunit ribosomal (rRNA) gene is present in every bacterial cell, serving as a universal marker. The gene is sufficiently conserved to allow accurate alignment but adequately varied to enable phylogenetic analyses. Sequencing via 16S rRNA-based phylotyping has been used to survey the bacterial microbes on the skin. Initially, we will examine the bacterial diversity associated with AD using a 16S rRNA survey and later broadening to include fungi, viruses, archaea and mites. In addition, bacteria will be cultured on a wide variety of media and isolates representing both abundant and novel species will be selected for whole genome sequencing.

To characterize fungal diversity, we utilize two phylogenetic markers within the rDNA region: 18S rRNA and the Intervening Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) region. Full microbial diversity will be explored with shotgun metagenomic sequencing.

assembly_info.comments: The assembly peDipJapo1.1 is based on 102x PacBio data and Arima2 Hi-C data generated by the Aquatic Symbiosis Genomics Project (https://www.aquaticsymbiosisgenomics.org/). The assembly process included the following sequence of steps: initial PacBio assembly generation with Hifiasm, retained haplotig separation with purge_dups, and Hi-C based scaffolding with YaHS. The mitochondrial genome assembly is mix of linear and circular contigs assembled with Hifiasm and identified via BLAST using mitochondrial coding sequences described in PMID 31919519. Finally, the primary assembly was analysed and manually improved using TreeVal. Chromosome-scale scaffolds confirmed by the Hi-C data have been named in order of size.

This alternate haplotype assembly combines the haplotigs separated by purge_dups with haplotigs separated from the primary assembly during curation.

attributes.name: project_name
attributes.value: Saanich Inlet is a seasonally anoxic fjord opening to the Strait of Georgia on the southeast coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia. It is approximately 24 kilometers long with a maximal basin depth of 234 meters and receives limited freshwater input from the surrounding watershed. A shallow glacial entrance sill 75 meters deep restricts circulation within interior and basin waters for most of the year. During spring and summer months, restricted circulation combined with high levels of primary productivity in surface waters lead to oxygen loss with concomitant water column stratification indicated by accumulation of methane (CH4), Ammonia (NH3) and Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S). In late summer and fall, oxygenated nutrient-rich ocean waters upwelling through the Strait cascade into Saanich Inlet shoaling anoxic bottom waters upward and transforming the redox chemistry of the water column. This process is stable on decadal time scales exhibiting a relatively narrow deviation in the depth distribution of the oxycline at different times of year. The recurring seasonal development of water column anoxia followed by deep-water renewal enables spatiotemporal profiling of microbial community structure and function across a wide range of water column redox states.

assembly_info.comments: The assembly pePerSpea1.1 is based on 40x PacBio data and Arima2 Hi-C data generated by the Aquatic Symbiosis Genomics Project (https://www.aquaticsymbiosisgenomics.org/). The assembly process included the following sequence of steps: initial PacBio assembly generation with Hifiasm, retained haplotig separation with purge_dups, and Hi-C based scaffolding with YaHS. Finally, the primary assembly was analysed and manually improved using gEVAL. Due to the poor HiC data quality, the assembly was submitted as curated scaffolds.
